newsitem.title: FRANCE: Embattled Eramet faces fresh New Caledonia woes.
newsitem.headline: Embattled Eramet faces fresh New Caledonia woes.

text.p: Eramet, the world's third-largest nickel producer, delivered on Tuesday more bad news to investors, saying local trade unions in New Caledonia continued to block its nickel metal exports.

The group, already caught in a dispute with the French state over the distribution of mining assets in the South Pacific island, said it could not ship a single tonne of ferronickel or nickel matte abroad.
But it said it was premature to declare "force majeure" on these export contracts although there could be problems if the situation continued.
"At this stage there is still no need to declare force majeure," a company spokesman told Reuters.
Local trade unions want to draw attention to their calls for a speedy solution to a controversial plan to build a nickel smelter in the north of French territory.
The French government, which owns 55 percent of Eramet, has begun the process to remove Eramet's mining licence for the Koniambo mine in New Caledonia.

It wants to hand the licence to local Kanak interests stating Eramet has not operated the mine for ten years. The Koniambo reserves would be used to supply a plant Canadian group Falconbridge Ltd FT.TO and local Kanak Societe Miniere de Sud Pacifique (SMSP) want to build in the north.
The project is part of a deal to appease Kanaks ahead of a 1998 referendum on independence for the French territory.
The government came up with the plan after talks between Eramet's Societe le Nickel (SLN) and the SMSP over an asset swap failed.
Eramet has said it would use all legal means to prevent the licence withdrawal, arguing it was unjustified and would hurt its financial outlook.
Eramet plans to produce 60,000 to 65,000 tonnes of nickel from the year 2000 from a current output of 54,000 tonnes.
Government has said there would be compensation for the licence loss. But analysts and industry sources say it would be unlikely to offset the revenue shortfall from the licence loss.
"If there is a compensation, it will be below the prejudice incurred and would force Eramet to cut down its whole development plant in New Caledonia," one analyst said.
There have been signs, however, that negotiations on mining asset distribution in New Caledonia might resume although no date has yet been set, industry sources said.
Eramet may provide an update on the situation when it presents its 1996 earnings at a news conference on Thursday, April 24.

But a snap parliamentary election in France announced on Monday may also put things on hold. "This will not help," one analyst said, adding the political situation in France was now adding to uncertainties plaguing the stock since last autumn.

One analyst said that Eramet's annual shareholders' meeting to be held June 19 will also be crucial for future developments. He said there were still concerns the government may seek to oust company chairman Yves Rambaud during the meeting.
Government officials were not immediately available for comment.
By early afternoon, Eramet shares were down 0.34 percent at 290 francs after having hit a session low of 285 francs.
